title: Type Checkers
text:
Pytifex runs four type checkers and compares their output to find disagreements. This page covers which checkers, how they get invoked, how their output gets parsed into “ok”/“error”, and how to add a new one.





Checker
Version
Command
Project




mypy
1.19.0
mypy <file>
mypy-lang.org


pyrefly
0.44.2
pyrefly check <file>
github.com/facebook/pyrefly


zuban

zuban check <file>
github.com/zubanls/zuban


ty

ty check <file>
github.com/astral-sh/ty



All four live in one dict in config.py:
CHECKERS = {
    "mypy": ["mypy"],
    "pyrefly": ["pyrefly", "check"],
    "zuban": ["zuban", "check"],
    "ty": ["ty", "check"],
}
Each value is the argument list that gets handed to subprocess.run, with the file path appended.



run_checkers.py walks every .py file in a generation directory and shells out to each checker:
def run_tool(command: list[str], filepath: str) -> str:
    try:
        full_cmd = command + [filepath]
        result = subprocess.run(full_cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=False)

        output = result.stdout
        if result.stderr:
            output += "\n[STDERR]\n" + result.stderr

        return output.strip() if output.strip() else "Success (No Output)"

    except FileNotFoundError:
        return f"Error: Command '{command[0]}' not found in PATH."
    except Exception as e:
        return f"Execution Error: {str(e)}"
A few things worth knowing:

check=False — a non-zero exit code never raises here. Most checkers exit non-zero whenever they find any type error, so the exit code by itself doesn’t tell you much.
stdout and stderr get merged into one string, with stderr appended after a [STDERR] marker.
A missing checker binary doesn’t crash the run — you get a readable error string back instead.

The results collect into results.json:
for tool_name, command in CHECKERS.items():
    output = run_tool(command, filepath)
    file_result["outputs"][tool_name] = output

file_result["statuses"] = {}
for tool_name, output in file_result["outputs"].items():
    file_result["statuses"][tool_name] = (
        "error" if checker_reports_error(output, tool_name) else "ok"
    )



Every checker formats its output differently, so there’s checker-specific parsing in _checker_reports_error(). That function lives in both comprehensive_eval.py and rederive_statuses.py — keep them in sync if you touch this.


Same format for both:
if checker in ("mypy", "zuban"):
    if "success: no issues found" in output.lower():
        return False
    m = re.search(r"Found\s+(\d+)\s+errors?\s+in", output)
    if m:
        return int(m.group(1)) > 0
    for line in output.splitlines():
        if re.search(r":\s*error\b", line, re.IGNORECASE):
            return True
    return False



Diagnostics start with ERROR. There’s a special case to filter out reveal_type() noise, which pyrefly reports as an “unknown-name” error even though it’s just a debugging call:
if checker == "pyrefly":
    real_errors = 0
    for line in output.splitlines():
        s = line.strip()
        if not s.startswith("ERROR"):
            continue
        if "unknown-name" in s.lower() and "reveal_type" in s:
            continue
        real_errors += 1
    return real_errors > 0



Clean runs print All checks passed!. Errors are lines matching error[rule-name]: — warnings and info diagnostics don’t count:
if checker == "ty":
    if "all checks passed" in output.lower():
        return False
    for line in output.splitlines():
        if re.match(r"\s*error\[", line, re.IGNORECASE):
            return True
    return False



A generic fallback for an unrecognized checker name:
output_lower = output.lower()
return (
    "error" in output_lower and
    "0 error" not in output_lower and
    "success" not in output_lower
)




If you fix the parsing logic, old results.json files still have statuses computed by the old version. There’s a script to recompute them — rederive_statuses.py. Run it as a module from the repo root, not as a bare script (it has relative imports):
python -m pytifex.rederive_statuses             # dry run, reports mismatches only
python -m pytifex.rederive_statuses --apply     # writes the corrected statuses
One caveat worth knowing: this script computes its ROOT as its own directory (src/pytifex/), but generated_examples/ actually lives at the repo root. So as written, the glob it builds (ROOT/generated_examples/*/results.json) won’t find your real output unless you run it with the working directory set to src/pytifex/ and a generated_examples symlink or copy sitting there too. If you hit this, it’s not you — it’s a path bug in the script, not something you did wrong.




Make sure it’s installed and on PATH.
Add it to CHECKERS in config.py:
CHECKERS = {
    "mypy": ["mypy"],
    "pyrefly": ["pyrefly", "check"],
    "zuban": ["zuban", "check"],
    "ty": ["ty", "check"],
    "pyright": ["pyright"],          # new
}
Add parsing logic to _checker_reports_error() — in both comprehensive_eval.py and rederive_statuses.py:
if checker == "pyright":
    # pyright prints "0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 informations" on success
    m = re.search(r"(\d+)\s+errors?", output)
    if m:
        return int(m.group(1)) > 0
    return False
Run the pipeline end-to-end to make sure it actually works:
uv run pytifex check
Sanity-check your parser against a real results.json. There’s a script for this too, check_checker_parsing.py — note it hardcodes a specific generation directory name inside it, so you’ll need to point it at one that exists before it’ll run:
python -m pytifex.check_checker_parsing

title: Architecture
text:
Pytifex splits its work across two places: an LLM API for generating and refining code, and your local machine for everything that has to be objectively true — fetching GitHub issues, running the actual type checker binaries, and executing the generated code to see what happens at runtime.
The important thing to understand up front: type checker output is always real. Pytifex never asks an LLM to simulate what mypy or pyrefly would say. Every status in results.json comes from an actual subprocess call to the real binary.







Where
What happens there




LLM API
generating code, refining examples that didn’t diverge


Local machine
GitHub mining, running mypy/pyrefly/zuban/ty, executing code to find runtime proof







Pulls closed, confirmed bug-fix issues from python/mypy, facebook/pyrefly, astral-sh/ty, microsoft/pyright, and zubanls/zuban. “Confirmed” means state == "closed" and state_reason != "not_planned" — this is the actual filter, straight from github_issues.py:
def is_confirmed_bug(issue: dict) -> bool:
    if issue.get("state") != "closed":
        return False
    if issue.get("state_reason") == "not_planned":
        return False
    return True
Code gets pulled out of fenced ```python blocks, and for pyrefly specifically, out of its sandbox links too (those encode the source as base64 inside the URL).



3-5 seed examples get shown to the LLM with a request to generate new variations likely to cause a disagreement. If there are no seeds (--no-github, or GitHub fetch failed), it falls back to a prompt built purely from the pattern descriptions in patterns.py. This is the actual branch in pipeline.py:
if seed_examples:
    prompt = build_seed_based_prompt(batch_seeds, batch_size)
else:
    prompt = build_expert_prompt(batch_size)
agent.py has three provider backends, each a small Pydantic model with a .communicate() method:








Class
Provider
How it’s picked




GetAccessToCohere
Cohere
--model starts with command


GetAccessToOpenAI
any OpenAI-compatible server
--openai-base-url is set


GetAccessToGemini
Google Gemini
default fallback — leftover, planned for removal



Right now, provider_for_model() falls back to Gemini whenever neither of the two conditions above matches, which is why omitting --model/--openai-base-url silently uses Gemini. That default is on its way out; don’t build anything that depends on it.
GetAccessToOpenAI just hits {base_url}/chat/completions — that’s it. It works against the real OpenAI API or any local server (llama-server, Ollama, vLLM) that speaks the same protocol.



Every generated example runs through all four checkers. If the resulting statuses aren’t all the same, it’s a disagreement and gets kept:
def has_disagreement(results: dict[str, CheckerResult]) -> bool:
    statuses = [r.status for r in results.values()]
    return len(set(statuses)) > 1



Examples where all four checkers agreed get sent back to the LLM along with the real checker output, with a prompt asking it to tweak the code minimally so it actually diverges. This runs up to --max-refinements times per example, feeding the latest refined attempt back in as context for the next one:
for i in range(max_attempts):
    prompt = build_refinement_prompt_for_example(current)
    response = agent.predict(prompt)
    refined = parse_into_example(response)
    refined.results = run_all_checkers(refined.code)
    if has_disagreement(refined.results):
        return refined
    current = refined  # next attempt refines this one, not the original



Every surviving disagreement gets run through a two-phase evaluation that decides which checker was correct. Covered in full on the Evaluation page — short version: Phase 1 catches runtime crashes, Phase 2 uses Hypothesis + beartype to fuzz the actual functions with type-conformant inputs. (The code still names these tier1/tier2 internally — see the note at the top of the Evaluation page.)




A few modules in src/pytifex/ implement additional evaluation strategies that aren’t called from the main evaluate_comprehensive() path right now — they’re either exploratory, used by other scripts, or superseded by the two-phase system:

source_analysis.py — pure AST analysis (no execution) that flags ~20 named PEP violations (LSP overrides, Protocol instantiation, Final overrides, TypedDict inheritance, etc.). It’s imported by comprehensive_eval.run_tier3(), but run_tier3() itself isn’t called from evaluate_comprehensive().
static_tier4.py — static flow analysis (import availability by Python version, variance violations, narrowing flow). Standalone, not called back into the main pipeline.
oracle.py — a cleaner architecture for matching source_analysis.py findings against parsed checker diagnostics.
checker_claim_verification.py — parses a checker’s specific diagnostic message (e.g. mypy’s Argument 1 to "f" has incompatible type "int"; expected "str"), synthesizes the exact “bad” value it’s complaining about, and calls the function with it to see if it actually crashes.
scoring.py — precision/recall/F1 scoring across tiers, used for writing up results rather than for the live pipeline.

If you’re trying to understand why a verdict came out a certain way, start with comprehensive_eval.py — that’s the only evaluation code that’s actually on the critical path.

title: Usage
text:
Run everything from the project root, with --extra dev so the type checkers are actually on PATH inside uv’s environment.
# full pipeline: mine -> generate -> filter -> evaluate
uv run --extra dev pytifex --model command-a-03-2025

# stop once you've found N disagreements
uv run --extra dev pytifex --model command-a-03-2025 --num-examples 10

# a local model behind an OpenAI-compatible server
uv run --extra dev pytifex --model qwen3-6b --openai-base-url http://localhost:8080/v1

# the real OpenAI API
uv run --extra dev pytifex --model gpt-4o --openai-base-url https://api.openai.com/v1

# skip GitHub seed fetching, generate from patterns instead
uv run --extra dev pytifex --model command-a-03-2025 --no-github

# verbose output
uv run --extra dev pytifex --model command-a-03-2025 -v

Triggered by passing --openai-base-url, regardless of model name. Works with real OpenAI, llama-server, Ollama, vLLM, or any server speaking /v1/chat/completions.

Needs COHERE_API_KEY or CO_API_KEY, triggered by any command-* model name.

title: Overview
text:
Pytifex finds cases where Python type checkers disagree with each other. It mines real bug reports from type checker repositories, uses them as seeds for an LLM to generate new code, runs that code through four checkers, and keeps only the examples where the checkers don’t agree. Then it figures out which checker was actually right, using runtime execution as the ground truth.


1. Mine seeds — once, up front, unless --no-github. Pulls closed, confirmed bug-fix issues straight from GitHub:
# github_issues.py
def is_confirmed_bug(issue: dict) -> bool:
    if issue.get("state") != "closed":
        return False
    if issue.get("state_reason") == "not_planned":
        return False
    return True
2. Generate — a batch of new code gets written by the LLM, seeded from those issues (or from the built-in patterns if there are no seeds):
# pipeline.py
if seed_examples:
    prompt = build_seed_based_prompt(batch_seeds, batch_size)
else:
    prompt = build_expert_prompt(batch_size)
3. Check — every generated example runs through mypy, pyrefly, zuban, and ty.
4. Filter — a disagreement is any example where the checkers don’t all return the same status:
# pipeline.py
def has_disagreement(results: dict[str, CheckerResult]) -> bool:
    statuses = [r.status for r in results.values()]
    return len(set(statuses)) > 1

title: Evaluation System
text:
Finding a disagreement is only half the job — once mypy says “ok” and pyrefly says “error” on the same code, something has to decide which one was actually right. This page covers the two-phase evaluation that does that.
(Note on naming: the code itself still calls these “tiers” internally — function names like run_tier1, the tier2_bugs list, and the "tier": 2 field in the JSON output below are all literal. This doc calls them Phase 1 / Phase 2 going forward; the rename in code hasn’t landed yet.)


Only runtime evidence counts. No heuristics, no PEP pattern matching, no LLM judgement in the verdict itself — a verdict only gets issued when there’s an actual crash or an actual successful execution to point to.

Phase 1 proves false negatives. A runtime crash is concrete proof a type error exists — any checker that said “ok” was wrong.
Phase 2 proves both directions. Hypothesis generates inputs that match the declared types (verified at the call boundary by beartype), then actually calls the function. A crash proves a false negative; a clean run proves a false positive.








Case
Proves




Phase 1 crash
checker that said “ok” is wrong (false negative), confidence 0.95


Phase 2 crash with type-conformant inputs
same, via fuzzing, confidence 0.85


Phase 2 success witness
checker that said “error” is wrong (false positive), confidence 0.90


neither
UNCERTAIN






Runs the code directly and catches the exceptions that actually signal a type error:
TYPE_ERROR_EXCEPTIONS = (TypeError, KeyError, AttributeError)
If it crashes, any checker that said “ok” has a proven false negative. If it doesn’t, Phase 1 has nothing to say and the result falls through to Phase 2.
It doesn’t just look at the top-level exception — it walks the whole traceback and follows exception chains (__cause__/__context__) to find the actual root cause, not just wherever the error happened to surface:
def _collect_chained_exceptions(exc):
    chain = []
    current = exc
    while current is not None:
        chain.append(current)
        current = current.__cause__ or current.__context__
    chain.reverse()  # root cause first
    return chain
It also re-executes every try/except body on its own, in isolation, specifically to catch errors that the code’s own exception handling would otherwise swallow silently.




Parse the AST to find every user-defined function and method.
Execute the source once to get a real, callable namespace.
Look up each callable’s signature and type hints with inspect and typing.get_type_hints().
Build a Hypothesis strategy per parameter type:
int           -> st.integers()
list[int]     -> st.lists(st.integers())
Optional[str] -> st.none() | st.text()
# custom classes get constructed recursively from their own __init__ hints
Wrap the call with @beartype. If a generated input somehow doesn’t conform to its declared type, beartype raises before the real function body runs, and that call gets skipped rather than counted as evidence either way.
Run @given tests and watch what happens.

A crash on type-conformant input (Phase 2a) is the same kind of false-negative proof as Phase 1, just found through fuzzing instead of one fixed example. A clean run (Phase 2b) gets recorded as a SuccessWitness:
@dataclass
class SuccessWitness:
    call_text: str          # e.g. "multiply(...)"
    calls_succeeded: int    # number of successful Hypothesis calls
    beartype_enforced: bool # True when beartype confirmed input conformance
A success witness is concrete proof the code is well-typed for at least one real call. Any checker that reported “error” on it has a proven false positive.
One more source feeds Phase 2’s bug list: targeted_tests.py. It’s not Hypothesis-based — it’s hand-written probes (empty tuples, NewType cross-contamination, decorator signature erasure, Protocol conformance, classmethod inheritance, and literally replaying the file’s own if __name__ == "__main__" block) that catch bugs Hypothesis’s generic strategies tend to miss. Its findings get merged into the same list (tier2_bugs in the code) before a verdict gets decided.

uv run --extra dev pytifex eval     # evaluate existing results only

  "method": "two_tier_objective",
  "summary": {
    "mypy":    {"correct": 8, "incorrect": 4, "uncertain": 3},
    "pyrefly": {"correct": 6, "incorrect": 5, "uncertain": 4}
  },
  "results": [
    {
      "filename": "protocol-defaults-1.py",
      "tier1_bugs": [],
      "tier2_bugs": [],
      "tier2_witnesses": [
        {"call": "render(...)", "successes": 30, "beartype_enforced": true}
      ],

        "pyrefly": {"verdict": "CORRECT",   "tier": 2, "confidence": 0.9,

      }
    }
  ]
}







Verdict
Meaning




CORRECT
caught every real issue, or correctly reported no issues


INCORRECT
missed a real bug, or flagged code that’s actually fine


UNCERTAIN
neither a crash nor a success witness — no runtime evidence either way



UNCERTAIN cases get escalated to an LLM judge as a last resort, which has to cite a specific PEP section for its answer rather than just guessing — but that only kicks in once both phases come back empty-handed. It’s not part of the core verdict logic above.
If you want to see what’s going on behind a particular verdict, every generated test (every Phase 1 crash reproduction, every Phase 2 property test, every targeted probe) gets saved as an actual .py file under generated_examples/<run>/tests/ — nothing here is a black box.

title: Divergence Patterns
text:
Python’s type system is spread across dozens of PEPs, and mypy, pyrefly, ty, and zuban each implement those specs independently. Where a PEP is ambiguous or just silent on an edge case, the four checkers make different choices — so the same valid Python code gets accepted by one and rejected by another.
These aren’t bugs in the usual sense. They’re divergences — places where a reasonable reading of the spec leads to genuinely different behavior. Pytifex calls these divergence patterns: recurring categories of type-system edge cases that reliably cause disagreements.
Why this matters:

Library authors need code that passes every major checker, not just the one they happen to use.
Checker developers can use divergences to spot spec gaps and places where alignment would help.
Anyone studying type system soundness needs an actual taxonomy of where implementations diverge, instead of anecdotes.




Defined as DivergencePattern instances in src/pytifex/patterns.py:
@dataclass
class DivergencePattern:
    id: str            # unique kebab-case id
    category: str      # grouping, e.g. "protocols", "generics"
    description: str   # what it tests
    pep_refs: list[str]  # relevant PEPs





Category
PEP refs




protocols
PEP 544



Protocol methods with default argument values. Checkers disagree on whether an implementing class has to use the same default or can pick its own.






Category
PEP refs




typed-dict
PEP 589, PEP 655



TypedDict mixing total=True/False inheritance with Required/NotRequired overrides. Combining a total=False base with a Required override in a subclass creates ambiguity about what’s actually mandatory at construction time.






Category
PEP refs




type-narrowing
PEP 647, PEP 742



TypeGuard/TypeIs functions with generic parameters, e.g. narrowing list[Animal] to list[Cat]. Checkers apply narrowing differently where container covariance is involved.






Category
PEP refs




callable
PEP 612



A ParamSpec-based decorator stacked on @classmethod or @staticmethod. How cls/self gets captured through the decorator is where checkers disagree.






Category
PEP refs




generics
PEP 673



Self as a return type inside a generic class with abstract methods. Tension between Self and the class’s own type parameters.






Category
PEP refs




newtypes
PEP 484



NewType values inside generic containers, and whether the wrapper preserves the base type’s variance.






Category
PEP refs




overloads
PEP 484, PEP 586



Overloaded signatures with Literal types that partially overlap. Checkers differ on which overload wins and whether the overlap itself should be an error.






Category
PEP refs




inheritance
PEP 591



A Final attribute in a base class replaced by a @property in a subclass. Some checkers flag this as an override; others allow it since a property is technically a descriptor, not a reassignment.






Category
PEP refs




callable
PEP 544, PEP 570



A protocol method with keyword-only params, implemented with positional-or-keyword params instead. Checkers disagree on whether that satisfies the protocol.






Category
PEP refs




generics
PEP 484



A TypeVar bound to a generic type (e.g. T = TypeVar("T", bound=Comparable[Any])), used inside another generic. Complex enough constraint-solving that checkers land in different places.




build_expert_prompt in prompts.py dumps every pattern description straight into the generation prompt:
def build_expert_prompt(num_examples: int = 10) -> str:
    patterns_text = "\n".join(
        f"- **{p.id}** ({p.category}): {p.description} [refs: {', '.join(p.pep_refs)}]"
        for p in PATTERNS
    )
    # patterns_text gets embedded in the generation prompt
This tells the model where to look instead of generating random type-annotated code and hoping. build_seed_based_prompt also throws in the first 6 patterns alongside the real GitHub seeds, as extra context.
Once a run starts: patterns go into the prompt → the LLM writes code targeting them → each snippet runs through all four checkers → only the ones where checkers disagree survive.



Protocol with a default value (protocol-defaults):
from typing import Protocol

class Drawable(Protocol):
    def draw(self, color: str = "black") -> None: ...

class Circle:
    def draw(self, color: str = "red") -> None:
        print(f"Drawing circle in {color}")

def render(shape: Drawable) -> None:
    shape.draw()

render(Circle())  # does Circle satisfy Drawable? checkers disagree.
Some checkers require the default to match exactly; others only check the signature shape.
TypedDict with mixed Required/NotRequired (typed-dict-total):
from typing import TypedDict, Required, NotRequired

class Base(TypedDict, total=False):
    name: str
    age: int

class Strict(Base):
    name: Required[str]  # override: make name required
    email: NotRequired[str]

def greet(person: Strict) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {person['name']}"

greet({"name": "Alice"})  # is 'age' required or optional here?
Final attribute overridden by a property (final-override):
from typing import Final

class Config:
    max_retries: Final = 3

title: Divergence Patterns
text:
Python’s type system is spread across dozens of PEPs, and mypy, pyrefly, ty, and zuban each implement those specs independently. Where a PEP is ambiguous or just silent on an edge case, the four checkers make different choices — so the same valid Python code gets accepted by one and rejected by another.
These aren’t bugs in the usual sense. They’re divergences — places where a reasonable reading of the spec leads to genuinely different behavior. Pytifex calls these divergence patterns: recurring categories of type-system edge cases that reliably cause disagreements.
Why this matters:

Library authors need code that passes every major checker, not just the one they happen to use.
Checker developers can use divergences to spot spec gaps and places where alignment would help.
Anyone studying type system soundness needs an actual taxonomy of where implementations diverge, instead of anecdotes.

title: Divergence Patterns
text:
Defined as DivergencePattern instances in src/pytifex/patterns.py:
@dataclass
class DivergencePattern:
    id: str            # unique kebab-case id
    category: str      # grouping, e.g. "protocols", "generics"
    description: str   # what it tests
    pep_refs: list[str]  # relevant PEPs





Category
PEP refs




protocols
PEP 544



Protocol methods with default argument values. Checkers disagree on whether an implementing class has to use the same default or can pick its own.






Category
PEP refs




typed-dict
PEP 589, PEP 655



TypedDict mixing total=True/False inheritance with Required/NotRequired overrides. Combining a total=False base with a Required override in a subclass creates ambiguity about what’s actually mandatory at construction time.






Category
PEP refs




type-narrowing
PEP 647, PEP 742



TypeGuard/TypeIs functions with generic parameters, e.g. narrowing list[Animal] to list[Cat]. Checkers apply narrowing differently where container covariance is involved.






Category
PEP refs




callable
PEP 612



A ParamSpec-based decorator stacked on @classmethod or @staticmethod. How cls/self gets captured through the decorator is where checkers disagree.






Category
PEP refs




generics
PEP 673



Self as a return type inside a generic class with abstract methods. Tension between Self and the class’s own type parameters.






Category
PEP refs




newtypes
PEP 484



NewType values inside generic containers, and whether the wrapper preserves the base type’s variance.






Category
PEP refs




overloads
PEP 484, PEP 586



Overloaded signatures with Literal types that partially overlap. Checkers differ on which overload wins and whether the overlap itself should be an error.






Category
PEP refs




inheritance
PEP 591



A Final attribute in a base class replaced by a @property in a subclass. Some checkers flag this as an override; others allow it since a property is technically a descriptor, not a reassignment.






Category
PEP refs




callable
PEP 544, PEP 570



A protocol method with keyword-only params, implemented with positional-or-keyword params instead. Checkers disagree on whether that satisfies the protocol.






Category
PEP refs




generics
PEP 484



A TypeVar bound to a generic type (e.g. T = TypeVar("T", bound=Comparable[Any])), used inside another generic. Complex enough constraint-solving that checkers land in different places.

title: Bug Mining & Mutation
text:
The core idea behind Pytifex’s generation step is: don’t ask an LLM to invent type-checking edge cases from nothing — mine real bugs from the checkers’ own GitHub issues and use them as seeds for new variations. A real bug report already proved a checker had a weakness somewhere; that’s a much better starting point than a cold prompt.
The pipeline never tests the original GitHub code directly, by the way. Seeds are inspiration only — what actually gets type-checked is always freshly generated code.




REPOS = {
    "mypy": "python/mypy",
    "pyrefly": "facebook/pyrefly",
    "ty": "astral-sh/ty",
    "pyright": "microsoft/pyright",
    "zuban": "zubanls/zuban",
}
Note that pyright is in this list even though Pytifex doesn’t actually evaluate pyright — its issue tracker just has a lot of useful code examples, so it’s a source for seeds, not a checker under test.



Not every closed issue is a real bug — plenty get closed as “won’t fix” or as duplicates. Pytifex checks the GitHub state_reason field:
def is_confirmed_bug(issue: dict) -> bool:
    if issue.get("state") != "closed":
        return False
    if issue.get("state_reason") == "not_planned":
        return False
    return True
Only state_reason == "completed" (or null, for older issues that predate this field) passes.



FALSE_POSITIVE_LABELS = ["false-positive", "false positive", "spurious", ...]
FALSE_NEGATIVE_LABELS = ["false-negative", "false negative", "missed-error", ...]
This classification gets passed into the prompt so the LLM knows whether the seed was a checker over-reporting (false positive) or under-reporting (false negative).



Two methods. First, plain fenced code blocks:
pattern = r"```(?:python|py)\n(.*?)```"
matches = re.findall(pattern, text, re.DOTALL | re.IGNORECASE)
Second, pyrefly’s sandbox links. These look like pyrefly.org/sandbox/?project=<base64> — the base64 payload decodes to JSON containing the source:
sandbox_pattern = r'https://pyrefly\.org/sandbox/\?project=([A-Za-z0-9%+/=]+)'
# url-decode -> base64-decode -> json parse -> pull out the code
Anything shorter than 50 characters gets thrown out as not useful.



60 requests/hour without a token, 5,000 with one:
export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_your_token
Or skip it entirely with --no-github.






Shows 3-5 real bug examples to the model and asks for variations:
prompt = f"""
## REAL BUG EXAMPLES FROM TYPE CHECKER ISSUES:
{seeds_text}

## YOUR TASK:
Using these real bugs as inspiration, generate {num_variations}
NEW Python code examples that:
1. Are VARIATIONS or EXTENSIONS of the patterns shown above
2. Target subtle type system edge cases likely to cause checker disagreements
3. Are self-contained and runnable (include all imports)

## STRATEGY FOR GENERATING DIVERGENCES:
- If a seed shows a false positive in mypy, create a similar case
  that other checkers also get wrong
- If a seed shows a false negative, create variations that test
  the boundaries of what gets caught
- Combine patterns: e.g., TypedDict + Protocol, ParamSpec + classmethod
"""
Every example the LLM produces has to reference a seed_issue (something like python/mypy#12345). Anything without one gets skipped during filtering.



If there are no seeds at all — --no-github, or GitHub was just unreachable — it falls back to build_expert_prompt, which drops the real issue examples and uses the pattern descriptions from patterns.py instead.



So you don’t get the same handful of seeds every batch:
start_idx = (attempt - 1) * 3 % len(seed_examples)
batch_seeds = seed_examples[start_idx:start_idx + 5]




results = run_all_checkers(example.code)
# {"mypy": CheckerResult("ok", ...), "pyrefly": CheckerResult("error", ...), ...}

def has_disagreement(results):
    statuses = [r.status for r in results.values()]
    return len(set(statuses)) > 1
If all four agree — either all ok or all error — the example goes to refinement instead of getting kept.



A non-divergent example gets sent back to the LLM with the actual checker output attached, asking for a minimal edit that makes a checker disagree:
def build_refinement_prompt(code, checker_results, seed_example):
    return f"""
    The following Python code was tested with all 4 type checkers
    but they ALL AGREED — meaning this is NOT a useful divergence example.

    ## ACTUAL CHECKER RESULTS (all agree):
    {results_text}

    ## YOUR TASK:
    Modify this code MINIMALLY to create a REAL divergence where at least
    one checker disagrees with the others.
    """
Up to --max-refinements tries (default 2). If a refined version diverges, it shows up in the output marked DISAGREEMENT (refined).










Flag
Effect




--num-examples N
stop once N disagreements are found


--batch-size N
examples generated per LLM call


--max-attempts N
generation rounds before giving up


--max-refinements N
refinement passes per non-divergent example


--no-github
skip seed mining, generate from patterns only


--model command-a-03-2025
a more capable model, usually a better hit rate

title: Overview
text:
What you need

Python 3.12+
uv — the only tool you need. It resolves and installs the project’s dependencies, and with the dev extra, the four type checkers too. No pip anywhere in this.
An LLM API key, unless you’re pointing at a local server that doesn’t require one.

title: Overview
text:
Fastest path
git clone https://github.com/benedekaibas/pytifex
cd pytifex

export COHERE_API_KEY=your_key

uv run --extra dev pytifex --model command-a-03-2025
--extra dev matters: mypy, pyrefly, zuban, and ty are declared as an optional dependency group in pyproject.toml, not a base dependency. Without --extra dev, uv run pytifex installs pytifex’s own two dependencies (pydantic, httpx) and nothing else — the checkers won’t be on PATH and every checker call will fail.
(One thing worth knowing right now: if you omit both --model and --openai-base-url, the CLI quietly falls back to Gemini — that’s a hard-coded default in main.py/agent.py that’s planned to go away. Until it does, always pass one of the provider flags below explicitly rather than relying on the default.)

title: Overview
text:
Picking a provider

OpenAI-compatible (real OpenAI, or any local/lab server)
Covers the actual OpenAI API and anything that speaks the same protocol — llama-server, Ollama, vLLM, or a server someone else handed you a URL for.
# real OpenAI
export OPENAI_API_KEY=your_key
uv run --extra dev pytifex --model gpt-4o --openai-base-url https://api.openai.com/v1

# a local/lab server — no key needed unless the server itself requires one
uv run --extra dev pytifex --model qwen3-6b --openai-base-url http://localhost:8080/v1
--openai-base-url is what forces this provider — the model name just has to match whatever the server itself calls it (check its /v1/models endpoint if you’re unsure).

title: Overview
section: What actually happens when you run it
text:
What actually happens when you run it
1. Seed mining — fetches closed, confirmed bug reports from mypy, pyrefly, and ty’s GitHub issues. Runs once, before generation starts.
2. Code generation — those reports go to the LLM as seeds (or the built-in patterns, if there are no seeds), which writes new code targeting the same edge cases.
3. Type checking — every generated example runs through mypy, pyrefly, zuban, and ty.
4. Filtering — examples where the checkers disagree get kept. Examples where they all agreed get one more shot: the LLM gets the real checker output back and tries to provoke a disagreement, up to --max-refinements times.
Steps 2–4 repeat in batches until --num-examples disagreements are found, or --max-attempts is reached.
5. Evaluation — every surviving disagreement gets executed under Phase 1 (runtime crash detection) and Phase 2 (Hypothesis fuzzing with type-conformant inputs) to figure out which checker was actually correct. Anything that comes back with no evidence either way gets escalated to an LLM judge as a last resort. Full detail on this step is on the Evaluation page.
Everything lands in generated_examples/<timestamp>/.

title: Overview
text:
GitHub rate limits
Without a token you get 60 GitHub API requests an hour, which runs out fast if you’re mining seeds repeatedly.
export GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_your_token    # 5,000/hour instead of 60
Or skip the mining step entirely and generate from the built-in pattern descriptions instead:
uv run --extra dev pytifex --no-github
